3.4.1.2-f100.accuracy_reason: The source is Juvenal 14.109: 'fallit enim vitium specie virtutis et umbra'.

3.4.1.2-f102.accuracy_reason: The Vulgate at 1 Corinthians 9:27 reads 'castigo corpus meum et in servitutem redigo'.

3.4.1.2-f109.accuracy_reason: The Vulgate uses 'pythonissa' or 'habens pythonem' for the witch of Endor (1 Samuel 28; 1 Chronicles 10:13), and the term comes from the Pythia at Delphi.

3.4.1.2-f12.accuracy_reason: Horace, Satires 1.1.69–70 has 'mutato nomine de te fabula narratur'. Calling Burton's phrase an echo of it is reasonable.

3.4.1.2-f129.accuracy_reason: In Burton's sentence 'Solus Rex' and 'Reipub. Finis' are separated by the parenthesis and the English words. Reading them together as 'the king alone is the end of the commonwealth' fits the context.

3.4.1.2-f152.accuracy_reason: This is the standard Catholic definition of the limbus patrum.

3.4.1.2-f16.accuracy_reason: In Plutarch (Lucullus 10) the south wind smashed Mithridates' siege engines, above all the great tower, rather than wrecking a fleet. The note also says nothing of Plutarch's 'Pontic trumpeter'.

3.4.1.2-f167.accuracy_reason: Critias 109b–c describes the gods dividing up regions and tending men like a shepherd's flock. The note rightly calls Burton's Latin a paraphrase.

3.4.1.2-f173.accuracy_reason: The preamble to Zaleucus's laws survives in Greek in Stobaeus and opens by requiring that inhabitants be persuaded the gods exist. The note's remark about the main text is accurate.

3.4.1.2-f175.accuracy_reason: Caesar, Gallic War 6.14 reads 'hoc maxime ad virtutem excitari putant, metu mortis neglecto'. Burton's 'ut … incitarent' does recast this as a statement of purpose.

3.4.1.2-f181.accuracy_reason: The prayer is traditionally given as Aristotle's dying words and is generally held to be apocryphal; the note hedges this properly.

3.4.1.2-f183.accuracy_reason: The half-line is Petronius fr. 27 and also appears in Statius, Thebaid 3.661. Burton's English does apply it to obedience.

3.4.1.2-f190.accuracy_reason: In Lucian's Necyomantia 7, Menippus describes the fruit-and-water diet and sleeping in the open that Mithrobarzanes prescribed. Burton quotes a Latin version.

3.4.1.2-f21.accuracy_reason: The closest wording is Curtius 4.10.7, not Tacitus, and the note correctly leaves the Tacitus attribution as Burton's own.

3.4.1.2-f27.accuracy_reason: The sidenote cites Cardano's commentary on Ptolemy's Quadripartitum (the Tetrabiblos), where Cardano does discuss the character of the different religions ('leges').

3.4.1.2-f3.accuracy_reason: The Vulgate at Isaiah 14:14 reads 'similis ero Altissimo'; Burton changes it to the third person.

3.4.1.2-f39.accuracy_reason: The words come from Gallic War 6.14. Burton's 'go from one to another' renders 'ab aliis post mortem transire ad alios', the rest of the sentence.

3.4.1.2-f44.accuracy_reason: Marco Polo's account of the Old Man of the Mountain (Aloadin) and his garden is about the Nizari Ismaili leader, and the identification is standard.

3.4.1.2-f49.accuracy_reason: Curtius 4.10.7 reads 'alioquin impotens, saeva, mutabilis, ubi vana religione capta est, melius vatibus quam ducibus suis paret'. There 'impotens' describes the multitude, so Burton's 'feeble women' is his own change; the note hedges this properly.

3.4.1.2-f51.accuracy_reason: The term comes from 'python', a spirit of divination named after Pytho (Delphi). The Vulgate uses 'pythonissam' for the witch of Endor at 1 Chronicles 10:13.

3.4.1.2-f59.accuracy_reason: These are Seneca, Troades 405–406, from the chorus beginning 'Post mortem nihil est'.

3.4.1.2-f62.accuracy_reason: Augustine, De civ. Dei 4.31, reports Varro saying that many true things are not useful for the people to know, and that it suits the people to believe some false things otherwise. That is Varro's view of the civil religion. Burton's English gloss does loosely recast it.

3.4.1.2-f68.accuracy_reason: Justin, 1 Apology 26, reports the inscription. The 1574 find of 'Semoni Sanco Deo Fidio' makes the Semo Sancus explanation the standard one, and the note rightly hedges it with 'probably'. Burton does break off with '&c.'

3.4.1.2-f69.accuracy_reason: Eudo (Éon) de l'Étoile was a Breton heretic of the 1140s, condemned at Reims in 1148.

3.4.1.2-f7.accuracy_reason: In the Ptolemaic system the primum mobile is the outermost sphere, and it drives the daily motion of the spheres inside it.

3.4.1.2-f8.accuracy_reason: In Laws 644d and 803c Plato calls man a puppet or plaything of the gods. The note says 'echoes', which is suitably hedged.

3.4.1.2-f86.accuracy_reason: Horace, Epistles 1.1.76, addresses the Roman people as 'belua multorum es capitum'.

3.4.1.2-f87.accuracy_reason: Seneca, De vita beata 1.3, reads 'pergentes non quo eundum est, sed quo itur', said of people who follow the herd like cattle.

3.4.1.2-f91.accuracy_reason: Implicit faith (fides implicita) means belief taken on authority without examining it. That is a correct gloss.

3.4.1.2-f92.accuracy_reason: Horace, Epistles 1.1.59–60, has 'at pueri ludentes "rex eris" aiunt "si recte facies"'. It is a children's game rhyme.

3.4.1.2-f97.accuracy_reason: The Vulgate of 1 Corinthians 8:1 reads 'scientia inflat'.

3.4.1.2-f99.accuracy_reason: Both scholastic terms are glossed correctly, and 'codigno' is clearly an error for 'condigno'.
